newsitem.title: NEPAL: Rift in Nepal government as foreign minister quits.
newsitem.headline: Rift in Nepal government as foreign minister quits.

text.p: Nepal's Foreign Minister quit his post on Wednesday in a serious rift with the ruling coalition's dominant communists over recent local elections.

Prakash Chandra Lohani said he had resigned from his post in protest against what he described as "widespread rigging and intimidation" by the communist United Marxist-Leninist (UML) party in May 17 and 26 local elections.
Lohani belongs to Prime Minister Lokendra Bahadur Chand's Rashtriya Prajatantra Party (RPP), which heads an uneasy alliance between royalists and communists.

Lohani later told a news conference that he met the prime minister and handed over his resignation personally. It was not immediately clear if his resignation had been accepted, or what effect it would have on the government.
Lohani said his party colleagues knew about his decision to quit but would not say if this posed an immediate threat to Chand. A regular session of parliament is due to begin on June 26.
"The (political) situation is fluid," Lohani said without elaborating. "It depends on how the government behaves."

Chand's RPP controls only 20 seats in the 205-member House of Representatives, the lower house of Nepal's parliament, while the UML holds 90 seats. The split parliament that emerged from general elections in 1994 has so far yielded three coalition governments.

Last month's voting for nearly 190,000 representatives in 4,000 village committees and 58 municipalities was marred by violence in which at least six people died. These bodies are the Himalayan kingdom's equivalent of local governments.
Latest results show the UML, the dominant partner in the three-month-old coalition, had won over 88,000 places while the RPP had captured only 21,000 places.
Officials have ordered re-polls in 437 places affected by violence, and full results are expected this week.
The main opposition Nepali Congress party which has won 50,000 places has also alleged widespread election fraud.

"This campaign of intimidation, threats and strong-arm tactics of the UML sustained by the help of the administration, found the RPP a silent spectator, helpless and without any defence," Lohani said in a statement.

"Basically, I had repeatedly suggested to you, Mr Prime Minister, that the political culture of treating the government as simply an extension of the party and the notion that the state machinery can be used to strengthen the party is a theme against democratic norms and values," Lohani's statement said.
He said Chand did not consider his "views as of any merit."

"I should have resigned even earlier than today but the Prime Minister of India was coming to Nepal and I was aware of the possibility of achieving progress in many areas of national interest during the visit. Therefore I decided to stay in my position until the end of the visit before tendering my resignation," Lohani said.
Indian prime minister Inder Kumar Gujral paid a three-day visit to Kathmandu last week. He was the first foreign leader to visit the kingdom since Chand took power in March.
The neighbours signed a pathbreaking agreement allowing private firms of both countries to produce and trade electric power, and signed a water sharing treaty.
India also agreed to allow traders from landlocked Nepal to cross its territory to reach ports in Bangladesh through a new transit corridor.
